title: Rashomon
events_chronological: A travelling priest passes the samurai Takehiro and his veiled wife Masako on the forest road.
The bandit Tajomaru, dozing under a tree, watches them go by and glimpses Masako's face when the breeze lifts her veil.
Tajomaru lures Takehiro off the path with a story of buried swords and ties him to a tree.
Tajomaru brings Masako to the clearing and forces himself on her while her bound husband watches.
Masako demands that the two men fight to decide which of them she belongs to.
Tajomaru cuts Takehiro's bonds and the two fight clumsily and in open terror.
Takehiro is killed and Masako runs from the thicket.
Tajomaru takes the samurai's sword and horse and leaves.
A woodcutter comes on the body in the undergrowth, runs to report it, and quietly pockets the valuable dagger.
A policeman captures Tajomaru by the river after the stolen horse throws him.
At the court Tajomaru boasts that he killed the samurai in a magnificent duel of twenty-three strokes.
At a temple Masako testifies that after the rape her husband looked at her with contempt, and that she fainted holding her dagger and woke to find it in his chest.
Speaking through a medium, the dead Takehiro says his wife asked the bandit to kill him, and that he took his own life with the dagger in his shame.
Sheltering from the rain at the ruined Rashomon gate, the woodcutter and the priest tell a passing commoner that they cannot make sense of what they heard.
The woodcutter admits he saw the whole thing and describes a squalid, cowardly fight in which both men begged and Takehiro died almost by accident.
The commoner points out that the woodcutter stole the dagger, which is why he lied to the court.
An abandoned baby is found at the gate and the commoner strips it of its clothes.
The woodcutter takes the baby home to raise alongside his own six children, and the priest's faith in people is restored.
syuzhet_notes: The film's present is the Rashomon gate in the rain, which it opens on at told-order bullet 1 and returns to for bullets 15-18. Everything between is flashback, much of it flashback inside flashback: the courtyard testimony is recalled at the gate, and the thicket is dramatised inside that testimony. Told-order bullets 5-11 are staged four separate times across the runtime, once per witness, with the facts changing every time; they are counted once here.
fabula_notes: The film refuses to settle which account is true, so any single chronology is a choice. This one follows the woodcutter's final version, generally taken as the least self-serving, and treats the four tellings of the thicket as one event set. Whether Takehiro was killed by Tajomaru, by Masako or by his own hand is never resolved.
